title: Arches National Park Travel Guide

hero.alt: Arches National Park sandstone arches and fins near Moab, Utah
hero.headline: Arches National Park Travel Guide
hero.subheadline: Plan Arches around Delicate Arch, Devils Garden, The Windows, Park Avenue, Fiery Furnace, ancient rock art, and the salt-and-sandstone geology behind more than 2,000 documented natural arches.

overview: Arches National Park protects one of the world's densest concentrations of natural stone arches, along with sandstone fins, balanced rocks, towers, slickrock, and desert washes. The shapes begin with much older geology: deeply buried salt deposits warped and fractured overlying rock, and erosion then exploited those weaknesses to isolate fins and eventually open arches.

A strong first visit follows the park road in zones rather than collecting photographs at every turnout. Give Delicate Arch its own hiking block, combine The Windows with Double Arch, reserve time for Devils Garden, and use Park Avenue or Courthouse Towers to understand the larger fin-and-monolith landscape. Heat, limited shade, parking, and timed-entry requirements when in effect should shape the day.

highlights.title: More than 2,000 documented arches
highlights.description: See openings ranging from tiny spans to Landscape Arch's extraordinary 306-foot light opening.

highlights.title: Delicate Arch
highlights.description: Hike to Utah's best-known free-standing arch and read the slickrock landscape that surrounds it.

highlights.title: Fins, faults, and salt geology
highlights.description: Understand how buried salt, fractures, uplift, and erosion prepared the rock for arch formation.

highlights.title: Desert cultural landscape
highlights.description: Connect Indigenous rock art, historic ranching at Wolfe Ranch, and the 1929 national-monument origins of federal protection.

thingsToDo.title: Hike to Delicate Arch
thingsToDo.description: Delicate Arch is the park's most recognizable landmark, standing alone on a sandstone ridge with the La Sal Mountains often visible beyond. Its opening is about 46 feet high and 32 feet wide. The standard trail is roughly three miles round trip and crosses open slickrock with little shade, making temperature and water more important than the mileage suggests. Near the trailhead, Wolfe Ranch and a nearby Ute petroglyph panel add human history to the hike. The arch's modern name appeared in print by the 1930s, but the landform is the product of vastly older erosion acting on Entrada Sandstone. Do not climb or carve on arches, and stay back from exposed edges around the viewing bowl.

thingsToDo.title: Walk Devils Garden to Landscape Arch
thingsToDo.description: Devils Garden contains one of Arches National Park's richest concentrations of fins and arches. The relatively accessible trail to Landscape Arch reaches an exceptionally thin span with a light opening of about 306 feet, among the longest natural arches in the world. A major rockfall in 1991 visibly changed the arch and reinforced the fact that these landforms are temporary. Strong hikers can continue toward Double O Arch and the primitive loop, where route-finding, narrow fins, sand, exposure, and heat make the experience far more demanding. Start early and distinguish the easy Landscape Arch walk from the much more serious extended loop.

thingsToDo.title: Explore The Windows and Double Arch
thingsToDo.description: The Windows section packs several large openings into a compact area, making it one of the best places to compare arch shapes without a long hike. North Window, South Window, Turret Arch, and nearby Double Arch formed along fractures and weaknesses in massive sandstone, but each evolved differently as pieces of rock fell away. Double Arch is particularly striking because two large openings share the same rock mass and were shaped partly by downward erosion from water collecting on top. Visit early or late for softer light and fewer vehicles, and walk the short loop rather than viewing the formations only from the parking lot.

thingsToDo.title: Walk Park Avenue and Courthouse Towers
thingsToDo.description: Park Avenue contains no famous arch, which is precisely why it is useful. A short trail drops between towering sandstone walls, fins, and monoliths that reveal the earlier stages of the same erosional process that eventually produces arches. Features such as Courthouse Towers, The Organ, and Three Gossips show how jointed rock is isolated into narrow slabs and towers. Walking the corridor makes the scale much clearer than a roadside overlook. Arrange a shuttle between trailheads if doing the route one way, or descend only as far as time and heat permit before returning to the upper viewpoint.

thingsToDo.title: Stop at Balanced Rock
thingsToDo.description: Balanced Rock appears to balance precariously, but the cap is not a loose boulder sitting on a pedestal. It is a harder block of Entrada Sandstone attached to a narrowing pedestal of softer Dewey Bridge material beneath it. Differential erosion has removed the surrounding rock faster than the resistant cap, creating the illusion of a delicately balanced object. A short loop circles the formation and gives different perspectives on its structure. The smaller companion known as Chip-Off-the-Old-Block collapsed during the winter of 1975–76, another reminder that the park's famous forms are continually changing.

thingsToDo.title: Enter Fiery Furnace with the required access authorization
thingsToDo.description: Fiery Furnace is a maze of narrow sandstone fins, slots, dead ends, and hidden passages rather than a maintained trail with obvious navigation. The name refers to the warm red-orange glow of the rock in low-angle light, not volcanic activity. Because the area contains fragile biological soil crust and complex terrain, access is controlled through ranger-led hikes or permits according to current park rules. Visitors should not treat a map line as a conventional trail. If you obtain access, move carefully through established routes, avoid stepping on dark knobby soil crust, and expect scrambling and route-finding rather than a simple scenic walk.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Wolfe Ranch and the Ute petroglyph panel
thingsToDo.description: Near the Delicate Arch trailhead, Wolfe Ranch preserves a small cabin and corral associated with John Wesley Wolfe, who settled here with his family around the turn of the 20th century. A short walk also reaches a petroglyph panel created by Ute people, likely in the 17th to 19th centuries, depicting riders and bighorn sheep. The juxtaposition makes clear that Euro-American ranching occupies only a recent chapter in a much longer human history. View rock art without touching it; oils from hands, scratching, chalking, or tracing can permanently damage cultural resources.

thingsToDo.title: Read the landscape from the La Sal Mountains and Salt Valley viewpoints
thingsToDo.description: Arches makes more sense when you look beyond individual formations. Viewpoints toward the La Sal Mountains, Salt Valley, and long sandstone fins reveal the large-scale structure responsible for the park. Ancient seas left thick salt deposits underground; later sediments buried them, and the mobile salt deformed, faulted, and fractured the overlying rock. Uplift and erosion exposed the Entrada Sandstone, while water, freezing, gravity, and time enlarged fractures and removed weaker material. Understanding that sequence turns every fin and arch into evidence of a continuing geological process rather than a collection of isolated curiosities.

bestTimeToVisit.title: Cooler seasons make exposed desert hiking easier
bullets: Spring and fall usually offer the most comfortable hiking temperatures, but they are also busy and popular parking areas can fill early.
Summer heat can make exposed slickrock dangerous by midday; start major hikes at dawn and carry substantial water.
Winter is quieter and can bring snow or ice that transforms the red rock but makes shaded trails and slickrock slippery.
Thunderstorms can produce lightning and flash flooding in washes; check the forecast even on otherwise dry desert days.

travelTips: Check whether a timed-entry reservation is required for your dates; reservation programs can change by season and year.
Start Delicate Arch and Devils Garden early to reduce heat and parking pressure.
Carry more water than the short trail distances suggest; much of the park has almost no shade.
Stay on rock or established trails and avoid stepping on biological soil crust, which can take decades to recover from damage.
Never climb, carve, scratch, or otherwise alter arches or rock-art panels.

faq.q: How many days should I spend at Arches National Park?
faq.a: One long day can cover the major scenic road and several short walks, but two days is better if you want Delicate Arch, Devils Garden, The Windows, and time to hike without racing between parking lots.

faq.q: How many arches are in the park?
faq.a: The National Park Service recognizes more than 2,000 documented natural stone arches in Arches National Park, with openings ranging from small windows to enormous spans.

Buried salt helped fracture and deform overlying sandstone into fins. Water, freezing, gravity, and erosion then enlarged weaknesses and removed rock from those fins until openings developed. Arches eventually collapse as erosion continues.

faq.q: Is Delicate Arch an easy hike?
faq.a: It is moderate rather than technically difficult, but the exposed slickrock, heat, elevation gain, and lack of shade can make the roughly three-mile round trip strenuous in warm conditions.
President Herbert Hoover established Arches National Monument in 1929. Congress later enlarged and redesignated the area as Arches National Park in 1971.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Arches National Park is a protected Colorado Plateau landscape north of Moab, not a city. Its defining landforms are natural arches, sandstone fins, towers, balanced rocks, and broad desert valleys.

sections.heading: Geography & geology
paragraphs: Deep salt deposits beneath the park deformed and fractured younger rock above them. Erosion later exposed jointed Entrada Sandstone, and water, frost, gravity, and time enlarged fractures in fins until openings formed. The same processes ultimately destroy the arches they create.

sections.heading: Indigenous and park history
paragraphs: People have traveled through and used this landscape for thousands of years, leaving archaeological sites and rock art that remain culturally significant. Federal protection began with Arches National Monument in 1929, and the area became a national park in 1971.

sections.heading: Outdoor & seasonal highlights
paragraphs: Walking, hiking, scrambling, photography, astronomy, geology, and ranger-led programs dominate visitor activity. Spring and fall are popular; summer heat requires early starts; winter can bring snow and ice to slickrock.

sections.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: A single paved park road climbs from the entrance and branches to major zones including The Windows, Delicate Arch, and Devils Garden. Build the day by area and avoid repeated backtracking to the entrance corridor.
